title: Baseball and the Color Line
bigQuestion: How did written rules, unwritten deals and separate leagues decide who could play professional baseball?

story.title: Two Papers in One Folder
story.kicker: A folder holds a big league's rule book and a ticket from a league that rule book never mentions.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz opens a gray archive folder on the table. Inside are two printed copies. The first is a major league constitution from the early 1900s. A constitution is the rule book that says how a league runs. It lists teams, fees, schedules and how owners vote.

The second paper is a copy of a ticket stub. It comes from the East-West All-Star Game at Comiskey Park in Chicago. That game began in 1933. Its players came from the Negro leagues, the leagues Black players and owners built when the major leagues kept them out.

A student named Marcus reads the constitution twice. "There is no rule here about Black players," he says. Ms. Ortiz nods. "That is the puzzle," she answers. "From the late 1880s until 1947, no Black player appeared in the major leagues anyway."

She lays a third paper beside the others. It is a list of years: 1867, 1884, 1887, 1920, 1947. "A line like this did not drift in on the wind," she says. "People drew it at certain meetings, on certain days. Other people crossed it on certain days too."

Marcus picks up a pencil. Beside each year he writes a question: who decided, and who was shut out? The ticket stub stays on top of the pile. It is proof that a whole league kept playing on the other side of the line.
story.think: Why might an unwritten rule be harder to challenge than a written one?

lessons.title: Clubs and a Convention
lessons.mainIdea: Early baseball was run by amateur clubs, and in 1857 New York clubs began a convention that grew into a national body.
reading: In the 1840s and 1850s, baseball in New York was a *club* activity. Members paid dues, elected officers and kept written rules. The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York wrote down its playing rules in 1845. Other clubs in New York and Brooklyn soon played by similar rules.

In 1857, delegates from New York–area clubs met to agree on one set of rules. The next year they took the name National Association of Base Ball Players. Historians shorten it to the *NABBP*. It was an *amateur* body. Its members were not supposed to be paid to play.

The Civil War ended in 1865. After it, the NABBP grew quickly, with member clubs from many states. Black Americans also formed baseball clubs in cities such as Philadelphia, Brooklyn and Washington. These clubs elected officers, wrote rules and scheduled matches, just as white clubs did.

words.d: a group whose members pay dues, elect officers and follow written rules
the National Association of Base Ball Players, the amateur national body begun in 1857
a player who is not paid to play

lessons.title: The Pythians of Philadelphia
lessons.mainIdea: In 1867 the Pythian club, a Black club from Philadelphia, asked to join the Pennsylvania baseball association and was turned away.
reading: The Pythian Base Ball Club was a Black club in Philadelphia, organized after the Civil War. One of its leaders was *Octavius Catto*. He taught at the Institute for Colored Youth. Catto also worked for Black voting rights and for the right to ride Philadelphia's streetcars.

In October 1867 the Pythians sent a delegate to the Pennsylvania state baseball convention in Harrisburg. The club asked for *membership*, the right to belong to the association and vote in it. White delegates made it clear they would vote no. The Pythians withdrew their application rather than lose the vote.

The Pythians kept playing. In 1869 they played the Olympic club, a white Philadelphia club. It is one of the earliest recorded games between a Black club and a white club. In October 1871 Catto was shot and killed in Philadelphia during election-day violence against Black voters.

words.d: a Philadelphia teacher, Pythian leader and civil rights worker, killed in 1871
the right to belong to a group and vote in it

lessons.title: A Rule Written in December 1867
lessons.mainIdea: In December 1867 an NABBP committee recommended keeping out any club with a Black member, putting exclusion into a written report.
reading: In December 1867 the NABBP held its national convention. Its *nominating committee* decided which clubs could be admitted. The committee recommended against admitting any club with one or more Black members. Its report said the aim was to keep political questions out of baseball.

This *exclusion* was written into a report. It did not name one player or one club. It named a whole group of people. No Black club in the country could join the national body, however well it was organized.

The NABBP did not last much longer. Some of its clubs began paying players. In 1869 the Cincinnati Red Stockings became the first openly all-professional team. In 1871 professional clubs formed their own league, and the amateur NABBP faded away.

words.d: a small group chosen to review and recommend who may join
keeping a person or group out

lessons.title: Walker in Toledo, 1884
lessons.mainIdea: Moses Fleetwood Walker played for Toledo in the American Association in 1884, when it was a major league.
reading: *Moses Fleetwood Walker* was born in Ohio in 1856. He studied at Oberlin College and played baseball there and at the University of Michigan. In 1883 he played catcher for the Toledo Blue Stockings, then a minor league team.

In 1884 Toledo joined the American Association. The American Association was then counted as a *major league*, one of the top professional leagues. On May 1, 1884, Walker played his first game for Toledo. He is recognized as the first openly Black major league player. His brother Weldy Walker played a few games for Toledo that summer too.

Walker faced threats and insults in several cities that season. An injury cut his season short, and Toledo released him in the fall. Toledo left the American Association after 1884. After the Walker brothers, no other openly Black player appeared in the major leagues until 1947.

one of the top professional baseball leagues

lessons.title: Two Decisions in July 1887
lessons.mainIdea: In July 1887 a star manager refused to play against a Black pitcher, and a minor league voted to approve no new Black players.
reading: *Cap Anson* was the captain and manager of the Chicago White Stockings, a National League team. In August 1883 he objected to playing an exhibition game against Toledo if Walker played. Toledo did not back down, and Anson's team played the game.

On July 14, 1887, the White Stockings were set to play an exhibition against Newark of the International League. Newark had a Black pitcher, *George Stovey*. Anson objected again. Stovey did not play that day.

In the same month, the International League's leaders voted to approve no new contracts with Black players. Black stars, such as Frank Grant of Buffalo, were playing in that league then. Within a few seasons, Black players were gone from nearly every white professional team.

Historians often name 1887 as the year the *color line* hardened. No law created it. It grew from many owners, managers and league officials making the same choice. Many Black players moved to all-Black professional teams, such as the Cuban Giants, formed in 1885.

words.d: captain and manager of the Chicago White Stockings who refused to play against Black players
a Black pitcher for Newark in 1887
the barrier that kept Black players off white professional teams from the late 1880s until 1947

lessons.title: A Line No One Signed
lessons.mainIdea: The major leagues kept Black players out from the late 1880s to 1947 through an unwritten agreement among owners.
reading: The *National League* was founded in 1876. Chicago club owner William Hulbert led the meeting that created it. The American League became a major league in 1901. Historians have found no written rule against Black players in either league's constitution.

Instead, owners kept a *gentlemen's agreement*. This is an unwritten promise that people keep without signing anything. Each owner simply did not sign Black players. When anyone asked, owners could say that no rule existed.

*Kenesaw Mountain Landis*, a federal judge from Chicago, was hired as baseball's first commissioner in 1920. A *commissioner* is the official with power over the whole sport. Landis held the job until he died in 1944. In all those years, no Black player reached the major leagues.

Black newspapers pushed against the line for years. Wendell Smith of the Pittsburgh Courier and Sam Lacy wrote about it again and again. In April 1945 Smith helped arrange a tryout for three Black players at Fenway Park in Boston. The Red Sox signed none of them.

lessons.title: Rube Foster's League, 1920
lessons.mainIdea: In February 1920 Rube Foster led team owners in founding the Negro National League at a YMCA in Kansas City.
reading: Andrew "*Rube Foster*" was born in Texas in 1879. He became a star pitcher and then a manager and owner. In 1911 he helped found the Chicago American Giants. The team played on Chicago's South Side.

Black teams had played for decades, but most had no league. Many traveled from town to town, playing whoever would book a game. This was called *barnstorming*. Schedules changed often, and players could jump from team to team.

In February 1920 Foster met other team owners at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri. Together they founded the *Negro National League*. It had a constitution, a schedule and a president, and Foster was its president. Its first season, in 1920, had eight teams, including the Kansas City Monarchs and the American Giants.
Foster led the league until illness forced him to step away in 1926. He died in 1930. The National Baseball Hall of Fame elected him in 1981. Many historians call him the father of Black baseball.

words.d: pitcher, owner of the Chicago American Giants and founder of the Negro National League
traveling from town to town to play games without a league schedule
the Black professional league founded in Kansas City in 1920

lessons.title: Owners, Offices and a Series
lessons.mainIdea: The Negro leagues were businesses with owners, offices and championships, run largely by Black owners and managers.
reading: In 1923 a second league formed in the East, called the Eastern Colored League. In 1924 its champion, Hilldale of Pennsylvania, met the Kansas City Monarchs in the first *Negro World Series*. The Monarchs won.

The first Negro National League ended in 1931, during the Great Depression. In 1933 a new Negro National League began. Gus Greenlee, owner of the Pittsburgh Crawfords, led it. In 1937 the Negro American League formed, and the Kansas City Monarchs joined it.

*Effa Manley* co-owned the Newark Eagles with her husband, Abe Manley, starting in the 1930s. She ran much of the team's business. She also backed civil rights causes. In 2006 she became the first woman elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame.

These leagues gave jobs to players, umpires, managers, bus drivers and sportswriters. They filled ballparks in Black neighborhoods. They were *institutions*: organizations with rules and officers that lasted beyond any single season.

words.d: a championship series between Black professional league champions, first played in 1924
co-owner of the Newark Eagles and the first woman elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame
organizations with rules and officers that last over many years

lessons.title: East-West at Comiskey Park
lessons.mainIdea: Beginning in 1933, the East-West All-Star Game at Chicago's Comiskey Park became the Negro leagues' biggest yearly event.
reading: In September 1933 the first *East-West All-Star Game* was played at Comiskey Park in Chicago. Comiskey Park was the home of the Chicago White Sox. Two months earlier, in July 1933, the same ballpark had hosted the first major league All-Star Game.

Fans chose many of the East-West players by *ballot*, a vote cast on paper. Black newspapers, such as the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier, printed the ballots. Readers filled them in and mailed them back.

The game became the Negro leagues' biggest yearly event. In the 1940s some crowds topped 40,000 people. Stars such as Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson played in it. It was held in Chicago nearly every year for decades.

words.d: the yearly all-star game of the Negro leagues, first played at Comiskey Park in 1933
a paper used to cast a vote

lessons.title: April 15, 1947
lessons.mainIdea: Jackie Robinson played his first game for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947, breaking the major leagues' color line.
reading: *Jackie Robinson* grew up in Pasadena, California. At UCLA he starred in four sports. He served as an Army officer during World War II. In 1945 he played for the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro American League.

*Branch Rickey* was president of the Brooklyn Dodgers. In October 1945 the Dodgers announced that they had signed Robinson. He spent 1946 with the Montreal Royals, the Dodgers' top minor league team. He led that league in batting average.

On April 15, 1947, Robinson played first base for Brooklyn at Ebbets Field. He faced threats and insults all season. He was named Rookie of the Year. On July 5, 1947, *Larry Doby* joined the Cleveland Indians and became the first Black player in the American League.

In 1997, fifty years later, Major League Baseball retired Robinson's number 42 for every team. Since 2009, every player and coach wears 42 on April 15. Robinson had been elected to the Hall of Fame in 1962, the first Black player chosen.

lessons.title: Twelve Years to Every Team
lessons.mainIdea: Major league teams opened their rosters one at a time, and the last did not field a Black player until 1959.
reading: Robinson's first game did not open every door at once. Each team decided for itself when to sign Black players. Some moved quickly, and others waited more than ten years. *Integration*, opening a group to people who had been kept out, came team by team.

Chicago's two teams moved at different speeds. *Minnie Miñoso*, born in Cuba, joined the Chicago White Sox in 1951 as their first Black player. Ernie Banks and Gene Baker joined the Chicago Cubs in September 1953. Banks later became known as "Mr. Cub."
The Boston Red Sox were the last team to integrate. *Pumpsie Green* joined them in July 1959. Fourteen years earlier, the same club had held the Fenway Park tryout and passed on Jackie Robinson.

As major league teams signed Black stars, many fans followed those players. The Negro leagues lost players and crowds. Many of their teams closed during the 1950s, and the last league ended by the early 1960s.

words.d: opening a group or place to people who had been kept out
a Cuban-born player who became the Chicago White Sox's first Black player in 1951
the first Black player for the Boston Red Sox, in 1959

lessons.title: Records Join the Record Book
lessons.mainIdea: Since 2020, Major League Baseball has counted top Negro leagues of 1920–1948 as major leagues and added their statistics to its records.
reading: For decades, the official major league record books left out the Negro leagues. Researchers spent years finding old games in Black newspapers. Many came from a *box score*, a printed table listing what each player did in a game.

The Hall of Fame began to change first. In 1971 *Satchel Paige* was elected through a special committee on the Negro leagues. In 2006 another special committee elected 17 more Negro leagues players and executives at once, including Effa Manley.

On December 16, 2020, Major League Baseball made an announcement. Seven Negro leagues from 1920 to 1948 would now count as major leagues. In May 2024 their statistics joined MLB's official records. Josh Gibson, a catcher for the Homestead Grays and the Pittsburgh Crawfords, became the career leader in batting average.
The Negro Leagues Baseball Museum was founded in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1990. It stands in the 18th and Vine district, near the Paseo YMCA where the Negro National League began.

words.d: a printed table listing what each player did in a game
a Negro leagues pitching star elected to the Hall of Fame in 1971
